questions.q: What pathological process underlies the consolidation seen in pneumonia?
ch: Fluid accumulation in the pleural space
questions.exp: Infection inflames the alveoli and fills them with exudate, impairing gas exchange. That alveolar filling is what produces consolidation on imaging.
why: Bronchoconstriction describes asthma and does not produce consolidation.
Alveolar wall destruction is emphysema.
Pleural fluid is an effusion, which is a different radiographic finding and may complicate pneumonia.
Arterial occlusion describes pulmonary embolism.

questions.q: Which organism is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
questions.exp: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common typical pathogen in community-acquired pneumonia.
why: Moraxella is a recognised typical pathogen but much less frequent than pneumococcus.
Viral causes are common but RSV specifically is not the leading cause in adults.
Mycoplasma is a common atypical cause, classically in younger patients, but not the most common overall.
Legionella is an important atypical cause but is far less common.

questions.q: An 84-year-old is brought in confused after a fall, with no fever. Which principle applies?
ch: Antibiotics should be withheld until fever develops
A normal temperature means the infection is viral
Pneumonia is effectively excluded by the absence of fever
Elderly patients may present with confusion or a fall rather than fever
Confusion in the elderly always indicates a primary neurological cause
questions.exp: Elderly patients with pneumonia may present with confusion or a fall and no fever at all. Suspicion has to stay high.
why: Waiting for fever delays treatment in a group where fever may never appear.
Temperature does not distinguish bacterial from viral aetiology.
Absence of fever does not exclude pneumonia in an older patient.
Confusion has many causes and infection is among the most common in this group.

questions.q: Which tool is used to decide whether a patient with pneumonia needs admission?
questions.exp: CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea above 7, Respiratory rate 30 or more, Blood pressure below 90/60, age 65 or over) structures the disposition decision. A score of 2 or more generally warrants admission and 3 or more prompts consideration of ICU.
why: Wells estimates the probability of pulmonary embolism.
GOLD grades COPD severity.
Child-Pugh grades liver disease severity.
The Glasgow Coma Scale measures consciousness, not pneumonia severity.

questions.q: A patient has pneumonia with hyponatremia, prominent gastrointestinal symptoms and a high fever. Which pathogen should be considered?
questions.exp: Hyponatremia with gastrointestinal symptoms and high fever in a patient with pneumonia is the classic Legionella pattern.
why: Influenza may precede bacterial pneumonia but does not produce this triad.
Pneumococcal pneumonia is typically an abrupt lobar illness without this electrolyte and GI signature.
Mycoplasma classically causes a walking pneumonia in a younger patient, sometimes with bullous myringitis.
Haemophilus is a typical pathogen, often in those with underlying lung disease, without this pattern.

questions.q: Cultures have been ordered but not yet drawn in a septic patient with pneumonia. What is the correct approach?
ch: Give antibiotics without delay, obtaining cultures if it does not hold up treatment
Withhold antibiotics until the chest X-ray is reported
Give antibiotics only after the severity score is calculated
Treat with antipyretics alone until cultures return
Delay antibiotics until all cultures are collected
questions.exp: Obtain cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but never delay antibiotics in a septic patient to get them. Timely first dose matters.
why: Treatment should not wait on radiology in a septic patient.
Scoring guides disposition, not the timing of the first dose.
Antipyretics do not treat the infection.
Delaying antibiotics in sepsis worsens outcomes.

questions.q: A patient hospitalised with pneumonia is not improving after 72 hours of appropriate empiric therapy. What should be considered?
ch: Repeating the same antibiotic course from the beginning
This is the expected course and no further action is needed
The wrong organism or drug, a complication such as empyema, or the wrong diagnosis
Immediate discharge on oral therapy with outpatient follow-up
Automatic escalation to empiric antifungal therapy
questions.exp: Improvement is expected within 48 to 72 hours. Failure to improve should prompt reconsideration of the organism and drug, a search for complications such as empyema or abscess, and a review of whether the diagnosis is right.
why: Repeating an ineffective regimen does not address why it failed.
Persistent illness at 72 hours is not the expected course and requires reassessment.
Discharging a non-responding patient is unsafe.
Antifungal therapy is not an automatic next step without specific risk factors.

questions.q: A parapneumonic effusion persists and is not resolving with antibiotics. What is the appropriate action?
ch: Repeat the chest X-ray in one month
Sample the fluid to exclude empyema, which requires drainage
questions.exp: A persistent effusion should be tapped to exclude empyema. Empyema needs drainage, not antibiotics alone.
why: Steroids do not treat an infected pleural collection.
Diuretics treat transudative effusions from heart failure, not a parapneumonic collection.
Waiting a month risks a loculated, harder-to-drain empyema.
Antibiotics alone will not clear an established empyema.

questions.q: What does antibiotic de-escalation mean in the management of pneumonia?
ch: Adding a second agent to cover resistant organisms
Stopping antibiotics as soon as the fever settles
Narrowing therapy once culture and antigen results identify the organism
Reducing the dose while keeping the same broad agent
Switching from intravenous to oral therapy regardless of results
questions.exp: Empiric antibiotics are chosen by site of care and risk factors, then narrowed once cultures and antigen results return. That is stewardship.
why: Adding an agent is escalation, the opposite of de-escalation.
Stopping at defervescence may truncate a needed course; de-escalation is about spectrum, not duration.
De-escalation narrows the spectrum rather than simply lowering the dose.
Route change is a separate decision from narrowing spectrum.

questions.q: Which oxygen saturation target applies to a patient with pneumonia who also has COPD?
questions.exp: The general target in pneumonia is at least 92%, but a patient with coexisting COPD is targeted to 88-92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia.
why: 96% or above risks CO2 retention in COPD.
Above 98% is unsafe in this group.
Oxygen always requires a defined target.
At least 92% is the general pneumonia target and does not account for the COPD.

questions.q: Where does the thrombus causing a pulmonary embolism usually originate?
questions.exp: A pulmonary embolus is typically a thrombus from a lower-extremity deep vein that travels to the pulmonary circulation, which is why PE and DVT are together termed venous thromboembolism.
why: Renal artery thrombus does not reach the pulmonary arteries.
Left atrial thrombus embolises to the systemic circulation, causing stroke rather than PE.
Carotid plaque embolises to the brain.
Pulmonary veins carry blood back to the left heart, so clot there would embolise systemically.

questions.q: Which triad describes the risk factors for venous thromboembolism?
questions.exp: Virchow's triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, travel), hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, thrombophilia) and endothelial injury.
why: Samter's triad describes aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
Beck's triad describes cardiac tamponade.
Charcot's triad describes ascending cholangitis.
Cushing's triad describes raised intracranial pressure.

questions.q: What is the most common ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
ch: ST elevation in the inferior leads
questions.exp: Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding. S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon.
why: Atrial fibrillation may occur but is not the typical finding.
Inferior ST elevation suggests myocardial infarction.
Complete heart block is unrelated to the usual physiology of PE.
S1Q3T3 is the textbook pattern but is seen in only a minority of cases.

questions.q: A patient has a high clinical probability of PE by Wells score. What is the correct next step?
ch: Send a D-dimer and image only if positive
Start warfarin and arrange outpatient follow-up
Send a D-dimer and discharge if negative
Proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography
Observe for 24 hours and repeat the Wells score
questions.exp: A negative D-dimer is only useful when pretest probability is low. In a high-probability patient, go straight to CT pulmonary angiography.
why: Making imaging conditional on the D-dimer is precisely the error in a high-probability patient.
Warfarin alone without a bridge is inadequate initial anticoagulation, and the diagnosis is unconfirmed.
A negative D-dimer cannot rule out PE in a high-probability patient.
Observation delays diagnosis in a potentially lethal condition.

questions.q: Which imaging test is preferred when CT pulmonary angiography is contraindicated by renal failure or pregnancy?
questions.exp: A V/Q scan is the alternative when contrast is contraindicated, such as in renal failure or pregnancy.
why: Coronary angiography images the coronary arteries.
Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the pulmonary circulation, though leg ultrasound may find the source DVT.
Cardiac MRI is not the standard alternative for diagnosing PE.
A chest X-ray cannot diagnose or exclude PE.

questions.q: How is confirmed PE risk-stratified to guide treatment intensity?
ch: By the absolute D-dimer level at presentation
By the size of the clot burden on CT alone
By hemodynamic status and evidence of right ventricular strain
By the patient's age and comorbidity burden
By the presence or absence of pleuritic chest pain
questions.exp: Risk stratification into massive (hypotension or shock), submassive (right ventricular strain but normotensive) and low risk is driven by hemodynamics plus RV strain markers, and it determines whether to thrombolyse.
why: D-dimer helps rule out disease, not stratify confirmed disease.
Clot burden alone does not determine physiological impact.
Age contributes to prognostic scores but does not define the categories.
Pleuritic pain reflects peripheral infarction, not severity.

questions.q: Which treatment is indicated for a massive PE with hemodynamic instability?
ch: An inferior vena cava filter alone
questions.exp: Massive PE with hemodynamic instability is the indication for thrombolysis, accepting the major bleeding risk that restricts it to high-risk patients.
why: An IVC filter prevents further embolism but does not treat the obstructing clot.
Aspirin is not adequate treatment for PE.
These are prevention measures, not treatment for an unstable patient.
A DOAC is first-line for hemodynamically stable PE, not for shock.

questions.q: When is an inferior vena cava filter appropriate?
ch: As a replacement for anticoagulation in stable patients
In any patient with a raised D-dimer
In all patients with confirmed PE
questions.exp: An IVC filter is used when anticoagulation is contraindicated. It is not a substitute for anticoagulation when anticoagulation can be given.
why: A filter is explicitly not a substitute when anticoagulation is possible.
Filter placement is not contingent on failed thrombolysis.
A raised D-dimer is non-specific and is not an indication for a filter.
Most patients are managed with anticoagulation alone.

questions.q: Which tool identifies low-risk patients with PE who may be suitable for outpatient management?
questions.exp: PESI and simplified PESI identify low-risk patients who may be managed as outpatients, a modern and cost-conscious option.
why: CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
GOLD grades COPD.
Wells estimates pretest probability of PE before diagnosis, not prognosis after it.
CURB-65 scores pneumonia severity.

questions.q: A patient with high clinical suspicion of PE becomes hypotensive before imaging can be performed. What is the most appropriate approach?
ch: Start oral anticoagulation and arrange imaging in the morning
Place an IVC filter before any other intervention
Wait for CT pulmonary angiography before any treatment
Treat the physiology, giving empiric anticoagulation or thrombolysis as indicated
Give a fluid bolus and repeat the D-dimer
questions.exp: In a crashing patient with high suspicion, empiric anticoagulation or thrombolysis may precede confirmatory imaging. Treat the physiology.
why: Deferring to the morning is unsafe in obstructive shock.
A filter does not relieve the existing obstruction causing the shock.
Waiting for imaging in a patient in shock risks death.
A repeat D-dimer adds nothing in a high-probability unstable patient.
